entry: Dedication speech by [[Abraham Lincoln]], delivered on November 19, 1863, at the Soldiers' National Cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, after the [[Battle of Gettysburg]]. Lincoln's 271-word address took under two minutes and followed a main oration by Edward Everett. It reframed the [[American Civil War]] as a test of whether a nation "conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal" could endure. Its closing words, "that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth," came to be viewed as one of the most influential statements ever delivered on the American national purpose.

[[Hot spring]] that intermittently ejects water and steam turbulently from a surface vent. Geysers are rare because they need heat, water and a plumbing system with the right geometry, conditions found mainly near active volcanic areas where [[Magma|magma]] lies close to the surface. Surface water seeps to an average depth of around 2,000 meters (6,600 ft), where it contacts hot rock. As the water boils, steam pressure forces a superheated column to the surface. Constrictions in the plumbing let pressure build, which distinguishes geysers from non-eruptive hot springs. Eruptions can change or cease through mineral deposition, earthquakes or human intervention. The name comes from Geysir, a geyser in [[Iceland]], meaning "Gusher" in Icelandic. Vapor jets on the moons [[Enceladus]] and [[Triton (moon)|Triton]], and on [[Mars]], are called cryogeysers, but show no evidence of the subsurface system that defines terrestrial geysers.

Indian poet, known as Mirza Ghalib, who wrote in [[Urdu]] and Persian. His Persian divan is at least five times longer than his Urdu divan, but his fame rests on his Urdu poetry, especially his [[Ghazal|ghazals]]. Born in [[Agra]] into a family of Mughals, he was given the titles Dabir-ul-Mulk and Najm-ud-daula by Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar in 1850 and was appointed the emperor's poet tutor in 1854. He lived through the decline of the [[Mughal Empire]] and the [[Indian Rebellion of 1857]], after which he never got his full pension restored. His fame came posthumously, though he had predicted that later generations would recognize him. Today he remains popular across the [[Indian subcontinent]] and among the Hindustani diaspora.

Ancient Sahelian empire in West Africa, based in what are now southeastern Mauritania and western Mali. Also called Wagadu, it was founded by the Soninke people and grew rich from trade in [[Gold|gold]] and [[Salt|salt]] across the Sahara. Its capital, Koumbi Saleh, was a commercial hub divided into Muslim and non-Muslim quarters, according to the Cordoban scholar al-Bakri, who wrote about the region in the 11th century. Ghana was the title given to its rulers, meaning warrior or war chief. After centuries of prosperity the empire declined and became a vassal of the rising [[Mali Empire]] in the 13th century, but its influence survives in urban centers throughout its former territory. In 1957 the Gold Coast, under [[Kwame Nkrumah]], took the name [[Ghana]] at independence.

Country in West Africa, officially the Republic of Ghana. It lies on the Gulf of Guinea and the Atlantic Ocean, sharing borders with [[Ivory Coast]] to the west, [[Burkina Faso]] to the north and [[Togo]] to the east. Its area of 239,567 sq km (92,497 sq mi) spans coastal savannas to tropical rainforests. The capital and largest city is [[Accra]]. The Akan are the largest of its many ethnic groups, though they form only a plurality, and most Ghanaians are Christians (71.3%). Ghana is a unitary constitutional democracy in which the president is both head of state and head of government. It became the first sub-Saharan African colony to achieve sovereignty, on March 6, 1957, and under [[Kwame Nkrumah]] it was influential in decolonization and the Pan-African movement. It is a founding member of the [[Non-Aligned Movement]] and a member of the [[United Nations]] and the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].

Long-snouted [[Crocodile|crocodilian]] of the family Gavialidae, native to rivers of the northern [[Indian subcontinent]]. Also called the gavial, it is among the longest crocodilians, with males reaching 3 to 6 meters. Adult males have a bulbous boss at the snout tip resembling an earthen pot called a ghara, which gives the animal its name. It is the most thoroughly aquatic crocodilian and leaves the water only to bask and nest. Females lay 20–95 eggs in sandbanks. Wild numbers have declined drastically since the 1930s, and the gharial now occupies only 2% of its historical range. It has been listed as critically endangered since 2007.

Form of amatory poem or ode, originating in Arabic poetry, that often deals with spiritual and romantic love. A ghazal is a short poem of five to fifteen self-contained couplets, called bayts, that share a rhyme (qafiya) and a refrain (radif). The first couplet rhymes on both lines, while the last, the maqta, often includes the poet's pen name. The form flourished in [[Persian language|Persian]] poetry in the works of Sa'di and [[Hafez]], and spread into the [[Indian subcontinent]] in the 12th century. It is now prominent in many South Asian languages, including [[Urdu]], and in [[Turkey]]. Set to music, the ghazal has become a popular genre in [[Malaysia]] and [[Singapore]]. Its central themes of love and separation allow an extraordinary variety of expression through allusion.

Port and university city, capital of East Flanders province in [[Belgium]]. It is Belgium's third largest city after [[Brussels]] and [[Antwerp]], with 270,473 inhabitants at the end of 2024. The city grew at the confluence of the Scheldt and Leie rivers and became one of the largest and richest cities of northern Europe in the Late Middle Ages. By the 13th century it was the biggest city in Europe north of the Alps after [[Paris]]. After the late 16th century it became less important, which left an extremely well-preserved historic centre. The ten-day Gentse Feesten festival draws about 1–1.5 million visitors each year.

Part of a city where people of a particular race, religion or minority group live closely together and apart from others, often because of political, social, legal, religious, environmental or economic pressure. Ghettos are often more impoverished than other areas of their cities. The term was first used for the Venetian Ghetto in [[Venice]], Italy, as early as 1516, where Jewish people were restricted to live. During the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]], more than 1,000 Nazi ghettos were established to hold Europe's Jewish populations as part of the [[Final Solution]] of [[Nazi Germany]]. In the [[United States]], the term has been used since the 20th century for poor neighborhoods of largely minority populations, especially African-American ones. The word [[Slum|slum]] is usually applied to poor areas of developing countries, while ghetto describes areas of developed countries that suffer from relative poverty.

British former socialite, convicted of child sex trafficking. Born in France and raised in Oxford, England, she earned a degree in modern history from Balliol College of the [[University of Oxford]] in 1985. After her father, the media proprietor Robert Maxwell, died in 1991, she moved to [[New York City]] and developed a close relationship with [[Jeffrey Epstein]]. She was arrested by the FBI in July 2020 on federal charges including sex trafficking of minors. In December 2021 she was convicted on five of six counts, including one of sex trafficking of a minor, and in 2022 she was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Soul or spirit of a dead person or animal, believed by some to be able to appear to the living. Descriptions range from invisible presences to lifelike figures, though ghosts are generally described as solitary, human-like essences. Belief in an [[Afterlife|afterlife]] and in the manifestations of the dead dates back to [[Animism|animism]] and ancestor worship. Funeral rites, exorcisms and some practices of spiritualism are designed to rest the spirits of the dead. A 2009 study by the Pew Research Center found that 18% of Americans say they have seen a ghost. Ghosts are not a scientifically testable concept, and ghost hunting has been classified as [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]]. Despite centuries of investigation, there is no scientific evidence that any location is inhabited by the spirits of the dead. Research suggests that some ghost sightings may be related to degenerative brain diseases such as [[Alzheimer's disease]], and some sleep aids, such as [[Diphenhydramine|diphenhydramine]], may rarely cause ghost-like hallucinations.

Superhot chili pepper cultivated in [[Northeast India]], also called bhut jolokia or naga jolokia. In 2007 [[Guinness World Records]] certified it as the world's hottest chili pepper, about 170 times hotter than Tabasco sauce and rated at more than one million Scoville Heat Units (SHU). It was superseded by the Trinidad Scorpion Butch T in 2011 and by the [[Carolina Reaper]] in 2013. Unlike most peppers, ghost peppers produce [[Capsaicin|capsaicin]] not only around the seeds but throughout the fruit. The species is *Capsicum chinense*, with some genetic material from *Capsicum frutescens*.

Abandoned or largely depopulated human settlement, usually with substantial visible buildings and roads. A town often becomes a ghost town when the economic activity that supported it, such as mining or farming, fails. Floods, prolonged droughts, war, pollution and nuclear accidents can also cause abandonment, as can epidemics such as the [[Black Death]] and the [[Spanish flu]]. Ghost towns are found on every continent, including [[Antarctica]]. The Americas contain thousands of former mining and railway towns, many in the western United States, [[British Columbia]] and Chile's [[Atacama Desert]]. A few have been repopulated through heritage tourism or pilgrimage.

Italian opera composer and leading exponent of the realistic verismo style. Born in Lucca in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, the sixth of nine children, he was descended from a long line of composers. He studied at the [[Milan]] Conservatory, where his orchestral Capriccio sinfonico was performed in 1883 and began his reputation. His early work was rooted in traditional late-19th-century Romantic Italian opera before it developed into verismo. His most renowned works are [[La bohème]] (1896), Tosca (1900), Madama Butterfly (1904) and the unfinished Turandot (1926), completed posthumously by Franco Alfano. Widely regarded as the most successful Italian opera composer after Verdi, his operas are among the most frequently performed and recorded in the repertoire.

Italian sculptor, architect, painter and city planner, credited with creating the [[Baroque]] style of sculpture. Born in [[Naples]] to the sculptor Pietro Bernini, he moved to [[Rome]] as a child, and Pope Paul V predicted that he would be "the [[Michelangelo]] of his age." As an architect and city planner he designed churches, chapels and public squares, along with elaborate fountains and funerary monuments. Among his sculptures are David (1623–1624), Apollo and Daphne (1622–1625) and The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa (1647–1652). The Fountain of the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona (1648–1651) and the colonnades of St. Peter's Square (1656–1667) exemplify his fusion of sculpture, water and urban design. Under popes Urban VIII and Innocent X he dominated Roman artistic commissions, and he also wrote and staged Carnival satires.

Greek-Nigerian professional [[Basketball|basketball]] player for the Miami Heat of the [[National Basketball Association]]. Born in Athens to Nigerian parents, he was selected 15th overall by the [[Milwaukee]] Bucks in the 2013 draft. He won consecutive NBA Most Valuable Player awards in 2019 and 2020, and Defensive Player of the Year in 2020. In 2021 he led the Bucks to their first NBA championship since 1971 and was named Finals MVP. He has received ten All-Star selections and was named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021. Forbes listed him among the world's ten highest-paid athletes in 2022 and 2024.

Humanoid being of folklore, often prodigious in size and strength. The word is first attested in 1297 and derives from the Gigantes of [[Greek mythology]]. Fairy tales such as Jack the Giant Killer shaped the image of giants as dimwitted, violent ogres that sometimes ate humans or livestock. Later writers, including [[Jonathan Swift]] and [[Roald Dahl]], portrayed some giants as intelligent and friendly. Giants often represent the human body enlarged to a monstrous size, reminding listeners of human frailty and mortality. In Irish legend, the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill is said to have built the [[Giant's Causeway]]. Claudine Cohen has argued that giant lore heavily influenced how people interpreted fossil bones of prehistoric megafauna. Some translations of the Hebrew Bible render the [[Nephilim|Nephilim]] as giants.

Hypothesis that the Moon formed when a Mars-sized protoplanet, called [[Theia (hypothetical planet)|Theia]], collided with the proto-Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. Canadian geologist Reginald Daly first proposed it in 1946, and debris from the impact later re-accreted into the [[Moon]]. It is currently the favored hypothesis among astronomers. Evidence includes identical stable isotope ratios in lunar and terrestrial rock and the anomalously high [[Angular momentum|angular momentum]] of the Earth–Moon system. The Moon's small [[Iron|iron]] core also fits the model. Several questions remain, including how the debris formed a single moon.

[[Bear]] species endemic to [[China]], with a white coat and black patches around the eyes, ears, legs and shoulders. Adults weigh 100 to 115 kg (220 to 254 lb) and are typically 1.2 to 1.9 m long, with males 10–20% larger than females. The giant panda is mostly herbivorous, eating almost entirely [[Bamboo|bamboo]] and bamboo shoots. A visible thumb on its forepaw helps hold bamboo, and it can digest starch. It lives in six montane regions of a few Chinese provinces, at elevations up to 3,000 m, and is solitary except in mating seasons. Farming, [[Deforestation|deforestation]] and development drove it from its lowland habitat. The Fourth National Survey, published in 2015, estimated 1,864 wild individuals aged over 1.5 years. It has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 2016.

Planet much larger than Earth, composed primarily of volatile substances rather than rock. The four giant planets of the [[Solar System]] are [[Jupiter]], [[Saturn]], [[Uranus]] and [[Neptune]]. Jupiter and Saturn are principally made of hydrogen and helium and are often called gas giants, although the term is misleading because most of their volume lies above the critical point, where gas and liquid do not separate. Uranus and Neptune, which consist of water, ammonia and methane, are classed as ice giants. The alternative term "Jovian planet" refers to the Roman god Jupiter. Objects above about 13 Jupiter masses, large enough to fuse deuterium, are classed as [[Brown dwarf|brown dwarfs]], though the cutoff is a rule of thumb. Many extrasolar giant planets have been identified.

Coastal area of about 40,000 interlocking [[Basalt|basalt]] columns in County Antrim, [[Northern Ireland]]. The columns formed when highly fluid lava cooled and contracted about 50 to 60 million years ago, during the Paleocene, and most are [[Hexagon|hexagonal]]. The tallest are about 12 meters high. [[UNESCO]] designated it a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1986, and it received nearly one million visitors in 2019. Legend credits the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill with building the causeway.

Deep-ocean squid, *Architeuthis dux*, of the family Architeuthidae. Estimates put the maximum body size at about 5 m (16 ft) for females, with males slightly shorter, and its feeding tentacles reach 10 m (33 ft). It is longer than the [[Colossal squid]] but much lighter. Claims of 20 m (66 ft) specimens are undocumented. It lives in oceans worldwide, usually near continental and island slopes at depths possibly of 300–1,000 m. Its chief predator is the [[Sperm whale]], and whales that attack it often bear circular sucker scars near the head. In 2004 a [[Japan|Japanese]] research team obtained the first images of a living specimen.

Star with a substantially larger radius and luminosity than a [[Main sequence|main-sequence]] star of the same surface temperature. Giant stars lie above the main sequence on the [[Hertzsprung–Russell diagram]], with radii up to a few hundred times that of the [[Sun]]. Ejnar Hertzsprung coined the terms giant and dwarf in 1905 or 1906 for stars of very different luminosity but similar temperature. A star becomes a giant after the hydrogen in its core is depleted, when hydrogen fusion continues in a surrounding shell and the outer layers expand and cool. Stars more luminous than giants are called [[Supergiant|supergiants]] and hypergiants. [[Arcturus]], an orange giant, has about 25 times the Sun's radius.

Parasitic disease caused by the protist *Giardia duodenalis*, especially common in children and travelers. Infection causes steatorrhea, a [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]] of fatty, sticky stools, with abdominal pain, weight loss and weakness. Symptoms usually begin one to three weeks after exposure, and some people have mild or no symptoms. The disease spreads by the fecal-oral route, when cysts in contaminated food or water are swallowed. Diagnosis is by microscopic identification of cysts in feces. Treatment typically uses tinidazole or metronidazole. Infection may cause temporary [[Lactose|lactose]] intolerance. In 2013 about 280 million people worldwide had symptomatic cases, and the [[World Health Organization]] classifies it as a neglected disease.

Small, tailless [[Ape|ape]] of the family Hylobatidae, native to tropical and subtropical forests from eastern [[Bangladesh]] to [[Indonesia]]. Called the lesser apes, gibbons differ from the great apes in being smaller, showing low [[Sexual dimorphism|sexual dimorphism]] and not making nests. Unlike most great apes, they frequently form long-term pair bonds. Their main locomotion, brachiation, involves swinging from branch to branch for distances up to 15 m (50 ft) at speeds as fast as 55 km/h (34 mph). They are the fastest of all tree-dwelling, nonflying mammals. The family has four genera and about 20 species, and its range includes the islands of [[Sumatra]], [[Borneo]] and [[Java]].
